questions.question: Show that for values of v << c, Lorentz transformation reduces to the Galilean transformation.
questions.answer: Lorentz: x′ = γ(x − vt), t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). When v << c, v²/c² ≈ 0 so γ → 1, and vx/c² → 0. Then x′ = x − vt and t′ = t — exactly the Galilean transformation. Relativity therefore contains classical mechanics as its low-speed limit.
questions.explanation: γ → 1 and vx/c² → 0 leave x′ = x − vt, t′ = t.

questions.question: If a particle could move with the velocity of light, how much K.E. would it possess?
questions.answer: K = (γ − 1)m₀c² and γ → ∞ as v → c, so any particle with non-zero rest mass would need infinite kinetic energy — impossible. Only a massless particle (photon) can travel at c, and it carries finite energy E = pc = hf, all of it "kinetic" since E₀ = 0. The question's premise is therefore physical only for m₀ = 0.
questions.explanation: Infinite K for any m₀ > 0; only massless particles ride at c with finite E = pc.

questions.question: Explain the difference between Special and General Relativity in simple terms.
questions.answer: Special relativity (1905) deals with observers in uniform motion (inertial frames) and no gravity: the laws of physics and the speed of light are the same for all, giving time dilation, length contraction and E = mc². General relativity (1915) extends the principle to accelerated frames and explains gravity itself: mass and energy curve spacetime, and free bodies follow the straightest paths (geodesics) in that curved geometry — gravity as geometry, not force.
questions.explanation: Special: inertial frames, flat spacetime; general: acceleration and gravity as curvature.

questions.question: Differentiate between Inertial Frames of Reference and Non-Inertial Frames of Reference.
questions.answer: Inertial frame: unaccelerated (rest or constant velocity); Newton's first law holds without extra forces; e.g. a smoothly cruising train. Non-inertial frame: accelerating (linearly, rotating); Newton's first law fails unless fictitious forces (centrifugal, Coriolis, pseudo-force) are invented; e.g. a braking car, a spinning platform. Special relativity applies only to inertial frames; general relativity handles all frames.
questions.explanation: Unaccelerated vs accelerating; fictitious forces appear only in the latter.

questions.question: Why can't any object move at the speed of light?
questions.answer: Because m = γm₀, p = γm₀v and K = (γ − 1)m₀c² all diverge as v → c (γ → ∞): pushing a massive object to c would demand infinite energy and momentum. Equivalently, velocity addition never lets successive boosts reach c. Only massless particles travel exactly at c.
questions.explanation: γ → ∞ at v = c: infinite energy and momentum would be required.

questions.question: What is the limitation in the Galilean Transformation Equation, and how did Lorentz solve it?
questions.answer: Galilean equations (x′ = x − vt, t′ = t) assume absolute time and simple velocity addition, so they make the speed of light frame-dependent and leave Maxwell's equations non-invariant — contradicted by Michelson–Morley. Lorentz solved it by transforming space and time together: x′ = γ(x − vt), t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), which keeps c the same in every inertial frame and leaves Maxwell's equations invariant, reducing to Galilean at low speed.
questions.explanation: Absolute time breaks c-invariance; Lorentz mixes space and time to preserve it.

questions.question: Calculate the value of γ (Lorentz factor) if the object is moving at the speed of light.
questions.answer: γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) = 1/√(1 − 1) = 1/0 → ∞. The factor is undefined (infinite) at v = c, which is precisely why massive objects cannot reach light speed.
questions.explanation: γ = 1/0 → ∞: undefined at v = c.

questions.question: State and explain the basic postulates of Einstein's special theory of relativity. Discuss length-contraction, mass variation and time-dilation.
questions.answer: Postulates: (1) the laws of physics are identical in all inertial frames; (2) the speed of light in vacuum, c, is the same for all inertial observers regardless of the motion of source or observer. Consequences: length contraction — a rod moving along its length measures L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²), shorter than its proper length L₀; time dilation — a moving clock ticks slower, Δt = γΔt₀, verified by muon decay and atomic-clock flights; mass variation — m = γm₀ grows without bound as v → c, so momentum p = γm₀v and no massive body reaches c. All three follow from the Lorentz transformation and merge into one consistent picture of spacetime.
questions.explanation: Two postulates ⇒ L = L₀/γ, Δt = γΔt₀, m = γm₀.

questions.question: Explain the concept of mass-energy equivalence. Derive Einstein's mass-energy relation and demonstrate that 1 atomic mass unit (u) is equivalent to 931 MeV.
questions.answer: Mass and energy are two forms of one quantity: E = mc². Derivation: for a body accelerated by force F, dK = F dx = v dp; with p = mv and m varying, v dp = v d(mv) = v² dm + mv dv. Combining with the relativistic mass formula m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²) yields dK = c² dm; integrating from m₀ to m: K = (m − m₀)c², so total energy E = K + m₀c² = mc². For 1 u = 1.6605×10⁻²⁷ kg: E = 1.6605×10⁻²⁷ × (3×10⁸)² = 1.4945×10⁻¹⁵ J = 1.4945×10⁻¹⁵/1.602×10⁻¹⁹ eV = 931.5 MeV ≈ 931 MeV.
questions.explanation: dK = c²dm ⇒ E = mc²; 1 u → 1.4945×10⁻¹⁵ J = 931 MeV.

questions.question: Discuss the important conclusions derived from General Theory of relativity. What are the experimental observations in favour of these conclusions?
questions.answer: Conclusions: gravity is spacetime curvature; light bends in a gravitational field; clocks run slower in stronger gravity (gravitational redshift); planetary orbits precess beyond Newton; gravitational waves radiate from accelerating masses; black holes and event horizons exist. Evidence: Eddington's 1919 eclipse starlight deflection; Pound–Rebka gravitational redshift and GPS clock corrections; the 43″-per-century advance of Mercury's perihelion; LIGO's 2015 direct detection of gravitational waves; Event Horizon Telescope imaging of M87* and Sgr A*; Gravity Probe B frame-dragging.
questions.explanation: Curvature, light bending, redshift, precession, waves, black holes — all observed.

questions.question: How does it principle of relativity differ from the classical Galilean view?
questions.answer: Classically, relativity of motion was accepted for mechanics but space and time were absolute: distances and time intervals were the same for all observers and velocities added linearly (u′ = u − v); Maxwell's electromagnetism was thought to hold only in one privileged (ether) frame. Einstein's principle extends relativity to all physics including electromagnetism and adds the invariance of c: space and time become observer-dependent (contraction, dilation, relativity of simultaneity), transformations are Lorentz rather than Galilean, and no privileged frame exists.
questions.explanation: Absolute space/time and an ether frame give way to invariant c and Lorentz transformations.

questions.question: Explain the concept of spacetime curvature in general relativity and how it is used to visualize the effects of gravity.
questions.answer: Mass and energy tell spacetime how to curve; curved spacetime tells matter how to move. Visualisation: a heavy ball on a stretched rubber sheet dents it, and marbles rolled nearby curve toward the ball — not pulled by a force but following the curved surface (geodesics). Real spacetime is 4-dimensional: curvature affects time as well, so clocks near mass tick slower and light paths bend. This geometry reproduces Newtonian gravity at weak fields and predicts lensing, redshift, orbits' precession and black holes.
questions.explanation: Rubber-sheet geodesics: gravity as geometry of 4-D spacetime, not force.

questions.question: Derive the basic equations of the Galilean transformation and explain how they relate the positions and velocities of objects in different inertial frames.
questions.answer: Let frame S′ move with constant velocity v along the x-axis of frame S, origins coinciding at t = 0. Assuming absolute time and unchanged lengths, an event at (x, y, z, t) in S has coordinates in S′: x′ = x − vt, y′ = y, z′ = z, t′ = t. Differentiating: u<sub>x</sub>′ = u<sub>x</sub> − v, u<sub>y</sub>′ = u<sub>y</sub>, u<sub>z</sub>′ = u<sub>z</sub> — velocities add linearly, and accelerations are equal in both frames, so Newton's laws are invariant. The equations thus translate positions and velocities between any two inertial frames — valid at everyday speeds but failing at v ≈ c.
questions.explanation: x′ = x − vt, t′ = t; velocities add, accelerations (and Newton) invariant.

questions.question: Discuss the Lorentz transformation equations in special relativity and how they describe the relationship between space and time coordinates in different inertial frames. Give examples to illustrate their application.
questions.answer: For S′ moving at v along x: x′ = γ(x − vt), y′ = y, z′ = z, t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), with inverse x = γ(x′ + vt′), t = γ(t′ + vx′/c²). Space and time mix: simultaneity, lengths and durations become frame-dependent while the interval and c stay invariant. Examples: a clock at rest in S′ measured from S ticks Δt = γΔt′ (time dilation, muon lifetimes); a rod at rest in S′ measured from S has L = L′/γ (length contraction); two events simultaneous in S′ differ in time by γvΔx′/c² in S (relativity of simultaneity); velocity addition u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²) keeps c invariant.
questions.explanation: x′ = γ(x − vt), t′ = γ(t − vx/c²): dilation, contraction, simultaneity, velocity addition.

questions.question: A particle of rest mass m₀ moves with speed c/√2. Calculate its mass, momentum, total energy and kinetic energy.

questions.explanation: Book prints [√2 m₀, m₀c, √2 m₀c², 0.41 m₀c²] — reproduces.

questions.answer: (b) Earth frame: t = d/v = 4.3/0.800 = 5.375 ≈ 5.38 years. (a) Travellers' clock: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.64) = 1/0.6 = 1.667, so t′ = t/γ = 5.375 × 0.6 = 3.225 ≈ 3.22 years (equivalently the contracted distance 4.3 × 0.6 = 2.58 ly at 0.8c).

questions.question: Differentiate between wave and particle.
questions.answer: A wave is a delocalised disturbance described by wavelength and frequency; it interferes, diffracts and carries energy continuously through space. A particle is a localised object with definite position, mass and momentum; it exchanges energy and momentum in discrete collisions. Quantum physics unites the pictures: light shows particle behaviour (photons, E = hf, p = h/λ) and matter shows wave behaviour (de Broglie λ = h/p, electron diffraction).
questions.explanation: Wave: delocalised, interferes; particle: localised, collides; duality unites them.

questions.question: Is it possible for the de Broglie wavelength of a particle?
questions.answer: Yes — every moving particle has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p = h/mv. It is physically meaningful (observable) when it is comparable to the spacing of a diffracting structure, as for electrons in crystals (Davisson–Germer). For macroscopic bodies λ is absurdly small, so the wave aspect is undetectable though still present in principle.
questions.explanation: Yes: λ = h/p for all matter; observable only when λ matches atomic spacings.

questions.question: Estimated Broglie wavelength of a cricket ball on the pitch?
questions.answer: Take m ≈ 0.15 kg, v ≈ 30 m/s: λ = h/mv = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/(0.15 × 30) ≈ 1.5×10⁻³⁴ m — some twenty orders of magnitude smaller than an atomic nucleus, hence utterly unobservable: the ball behaves purely as a particle.
questions.explanation: ≈10⁻³⁴ m: far beyond any possible detection.

questions.question: Differentiate between the continuous and discrete emission of radiation?
questions.answer: Continuous emission: a hot dense body radiates a smooth spectrum of all wavelengths (black-body curve), classically pictured as uninterrupted wave emission. Discrete emission: atoms emit only certain photon energies hf = E₂ − E₁ between quantised levels, giving line spectra; energy leaves in indivisible quanta. Planck's quantisation reconciles the two: the black-body curve is the statistical sum of discrete oscillator emissions.
questions.explanation: Smooth black-body spectrum vs quantised line emission (hf per photon).

questions.question: What is threshold frequency?
questions.answer: The threshold frequency f₀ is the minimum frequency of incident light that can eject photoelectrons from a given surface: hf₀ = φ (the work function). Below f₀ no emission occurs at any intensity; above it, K<sub>max</sub> = h(f − f₀) grows linearly with f.
questions.explanation: f₀ = φ/h: the minimum frequency for emission.

questions.question: How has the photoelectric effect been applied in real-world technologies or devices, and what are its practical implications?
questions.answer: Devices: photodiodes and phototransistors, solar cells, photomultiplier tubes, camera light meters, burglar alarms and automatic doors (beam interruption), sound tracks on film, night-vision and image intensifiers, photoelectron spectroscopy. Implications: it established light quanta (E = hf), the work-function concept and the frequency (not intensity) dependence of electron energy — the cornerstone of quantum theory and of all optoelectronics.
questions.explanation: Photocells, solar cells, PMTs, sensors; proof of photons and of quantum theory.

questions.question: What are the advantages of an electron microscope over an optical microscope?
questions.answer: Resolution is limited by wavelength: electrons accelerated through tens of kV have λ ≈ 10⁻¹²–10⁻¹¹ m, thousands of times smaller than visible light (4–7×10⁻⁷ m), so an electron microscope resolves nanometre and atomic detail (≈0.1 nm) against ≈200 nm for light. Electromagnetic lenses give magnifications beyond ×10⁶, and the beam can be scanned or diffracted for compositional and structural information. Cost: vacuum, thin specimens, no live imaging.
questions.explanation: Picometre electron wavelengths beat light's diffraction limit by ~1000×.

questions.question: Is it possible to create only an electron through matter and photon interaction?
questions.answer: No. A photon interacting with matter cannot create a single electron: electric charge and lepton number must be conserved, and an electron carries charge −e and lepton number +1 while the photon carries neither. Pair production therefore always yields an electron–positron pair (near a nucleus to absorb momentum); a photon can only transfer energy to, or eject, an electron that already exists.
questions.explanation: No — charge and lepton number conservation force pair (e⁻e⁺) creation.

questions.question: Give construction of electron microscope?
questions.answer: An evacuated column contains: an electron gun (heated cathode + accelerating anode, tens of kV); a condenser electromagnetic lens focusing the beam onto the specimen; a thin specimen stage; an objective lens forming the first magnified image; a projector lens enlarging it further; and a fluorescent screen or CCD to display the final image. Electromagnetic coils (not glass) focus because electrons are charged; the vacuum prevents scattering by air.
questions.explanation: Gun → condenser → specimen → objective → projector → screen, all magnetic lenses in vacuum.

questions.question: Elaborate the particle nature of electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: EM radiation exchanges energy in quanta: E = hf per photon, momentum p = E/c = h/λ. Evidence: the photoelectric effect (threshold frequency, instantaneous emission, K<sub>max</sub> ∝ f), Compton scattering (photon–electron collisions conserving energy and momentum with Δλ = λ<sub>c</sub>(1 − cosθ)), black-body radiation (Planck's oscillators), and pair production (hf → e⁻e⁺). Intensity is photon flux; the wave field gives probabilities while detection events are discrete particles.
questions.explanation: Photons with E = hf, p = h/λ explain photoelectric, Compton, Planck and pair production.

questions.question: Describe how energy is distributed over the wavelength range for different temperatures.
questions.answer: A black body emits a continuous spectrum: at each temperature the intensity rises with λ, peaks at λ<sub>m</sub>, then falls. Raising T raises every ordinate, so the total power (∝ T⁴, Stefan–Boltzmann) grows and the peak shifts to shorter λ (λ<sub>m</sub>T = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K, Wien) — a hot body glows red, then white, then blue-white. Classical theory (Rayleigh–Jeans) matched only long wavelengths and diverged at short ones (ultraviolet catastrophe); Planck's quantised oscillators reproduce the whole family of curves.
questions.explanation: Black-body curves: area ∝ T⁴, peak ∝ 1/T; Planck fixes the ultraviolet catastrophe.

questions.question: Explain the particle model of light in terms of photons with particular energy and frequency.
questions.answer: Light of frequency f is a stream of photons, each carrying energy E = hf and momentum p = h/λ = hf/c; a beam's intensity is the photon flux times hf. The model explains the photoelectric effect (one photon frees one electron; K<sub>max</sub> = hf − φ; threshold f₀ = φ/h; emission instantaneous), Compton scattering (photon–electron billiards), and pair production, all of which defeat the pure wave picture, while interference and diffraction remain wave phenomena — hence wave–particle duality.
questions.explanation: Photons: E = hf, p = h/λ; intensity = flux × hf.

questions.question: Describe conservation laws in pair production and annihilation of matter.
questions.answer: Pair production: a photon of energy hf ≥ 2m₀c² = 1.022 MeV, near a nucleus, converts into an electron–positron pair. Conserved: energy (hf = 2m₀c² + K), momentum (the nucleus recoils to balance), electric charge (0 → +e − e), lepton number (0 → +1 − 1). Annihilation: e⁻ + e⁺ → two photons (usually), each 0.511 MeV for slow pairs; two photons (not one) are required so that momentum is conserved in the centre-of-mass frame; charge and lepton number return to zero. Matter and energy interconvert exactly per E = mc².
questions.explanation: Energy, momentum, charge and lepton number conserved in both directions.

questions.question: Describe Compton's effect qualitatively.
questions.answer: When X-rays scatter off loosely bound (essentially free) electrons, the scattered beam contains a longer wavelength alongside the original one. Picture the photon as a particle colliding elastically with an electron: it transfers part of its energy and momentum, so the scattered photon has less energy, lower frequency and longer wavelength; the electron recoils. The shift Δλ = λ<sub>c</sub>(1 − cosθ) depends only on scattering angle, not on material or incident wavelength — direct evidence that photons carry momentum h/λ.
questions.explanation: Photon–electron collision: scattered photon red-shifted by λ<sub>c</sub>(1 − cosθ).

questions.question: Explain how the very short wavelength of electrons, and the ability to use electrons and magnetic fields to focus them, allows electron microscope to achieve very high resolution.
questions.answer: Resolution cannot be finer than roughly the probing wavelength. Electrons accelerated through V have λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.23/√V nm: at 100 kV, λ ≈ 0.0037 nm, about 10⁵ times shorter than visible light, so the diffraction-limited spot is atomic-scale. Because electrons are charged, magnetic (electromagnetic) lenses bend and focus them like glass focuses light, forming condenser, objective and projector stages that magnify without touching the specimen. Short λ plus lensable charge gives sub-nanometre resolution.
questions.explanation: λ ≈ pm at tens of kV; magnetic lenses focus the charged beam ⇒ atomic resolution.

questions.question: Describe the impact of de Broglie proposal that any kind of particle has both wave and particle properties.
questions.answer: De Broglie (1924) assigned λ = h/p to every particle, symmetrising wave–particle duality. Impact: Schrödinger built wave mechanics on it (quantised states as standing waves, explaining atomic levels); Davisson–Germer and G.P. Thomson observed electron diffraction, confirming it; technology followed — electron microscopy, neutron diffraction for structures, atom interferometry; conceptually it forced the probabilistic (Born) interpretation and the uncertainty principle, reshaping all of microscopic physics.
questions.explanation: Matter waves ⇒ wave mechanics, diffraction confirmation, microscopes, uncertainty.

questions.question: Describe the confirmation of de Broglie proposal by Davisson and Germer experiment in which the diffraction of electrons by the surface layers of a crystal lattice was observed.
questions.answer: Davisson and Germer fired a beam of electrons (accelerating voltage V) at a nickel crystal and measured the scattered intensity versus angle. At V = 54 V a strong peak appeared at θ = 50°, exactly where Bragg's law nλ = 2d sinφ places a diffraction maximum for the Ni lattice spacing — with λ equal to de Broglie's h/p (≈0.165 nm), not any classical value. Varying V moved the peaks as λ = h/√(2meV) predicts. Electrons were diffracting like waves: matter waves confirmed.
questions.explanation: Ni-crystal peak at 54 V, 50° matched Bragg with λ = h/p.

questions.question: The Sun's surface temperature is 5700 K. (i) How much power is radiated by the Sun? (ii) Given that the distance to Earth is about 200 Sun radii, what is the maximum power possible from one square kilometer solar energy installation? (iii) What is the wavelength of maximum intensity of solar radiation?
questions.answer: Surface flux σT⁴ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ × 5700⁴ = 5.98×10⁷ W/m². (i) P = σT⁴ × 4πR² = 5.98×10⁷ × 4π(6.96×10⁸)² = 3.6×10²⁶ W. (ii) At Earth the flux is diluted by (R/d)² = (1/200)²: I = 5.98×10⁷/4×10⁴ = 1.5×10³ W/m²; over 1 km² (10⁶ m²) the maximum power = 1.5×10⁹ W. (iii) λ<sub>m</sub> = 2.898×10⁻³/5700 = 5.1×10⁻⁷ m.
questions.explanation: Book prints (5.98×10⁷ W/m², 3.6×10²⁶ Watts, 5.1×10⁻⁷ m) — (i) and (iii) reproduce; the part-(ii) value (1.5×10⁹ W) is not printed, the tag listing the surface flux instead. Flagged.

When the incident light has a frequency of 1.2×10¹⁴ Hz, the stopping potential is measured as −0.16 V. Estimate a value of Planck's constant from these data and determine the percentage error of your estimation.

questions.question: X-rays with an energy of 300 keV undergo Compton scattering with a target. If the scattered X-rays are detected at 30° relative to the incident X-rays, determine the Compton shift at this angle, the energy of the scattered X-rays, and the energy of the recoiling electron.
questions.answer: Δλ = λ<sub>c</sub>(1 − cos30°) = 2.43 pm × 0.1340 = 0.326 pm. λ = hc/E = 1240 eV·nm/300 keV = 4.13 pm; λ′ = 4.13 + 0.33 = 4.46 pm ⇒ E′ = 278 keV; recoil electron K = 300 − 278 = 22 keV.

questions.question: A photon with a wavelength of 6.0×10⁻¹² m collides with an electron. After the collision the photon wavelength is found to have been changed by exactly one Compton wavelength (2.43×10⁻¹² m). (i) What is the photon's wavelength after collision? (ii) Through what angle has been deflected in this collision? (iii) What is the angle for the electron after the collision? (iv) What is the electron's kinetic energy, in eV, after collision?
questions.answer: (i) λ′ = 6.0 + 2.43 = 8.43×10⁻¹² m ≈ 8.4×10⁻¹² m. (ii) Δλ = λ<sub>c</sub>(1 − cosθ) = λ<sub>c</sub> ⇒ cosθ = 0 ⇒ θ = 90°. (iii) cotφ = (1 + hf/m₀c²) tan(θ/2) = (1 + 206.7/511)(1) = 1.404 ⇒ φ = 35.5°, i.e. less than 90°. (iv) K = hc/λ − hc/λ′ = 206.7 − 147.1 = 59.6 keV ≈ 5.9×10⁴ eV.

questions.question: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron in the ground state of hydrogen.

questions.question: Why do different elements have different spectra?
questions.answer: Each element possesses its own unique set of quantised energy levels, fixed by its nuclear charge and electron configuration. The photon energies hf = E<sub>i</sub> − E<sub>f</sub>, and hence the wavelengths, of its transitions therefore differ from element to element, so every element emits and absorbs its own characteristic line spectrum — a spectral fingerprint.

questions.question: In the Bohr model, how many times larger is the radius of the fifth Bohr orbit compared to that of the first Bohr orbit?
questions.answer: r<sub>n</sub> = n²a₀ ⇒ r₅/r₁ = 5²/1² = 25. The fifth orbit is 25 times larger than the first.

questions.question: What is the difference between X-Rays and Gamma Rays?
questions.answer: Both are electromagnetic waves, but they differ in origin: X-rays arise from extranuclear processes — bremsstrahlung of decelerating fast electrons and inner-shell electron transitions — with wavelengths ≈0.01–10 nm and a continuous-plus-characteristic-line spectrum; gamma rays arise from nuclear transitions (radioactive decay, nuclear reactions), are typically more energetic and form discrete lines. Where the wavelength ranges overlap, only the origin distinguishes them.

questions.question: Sate the properties of X-Rays, which makes it possible to detect cracks in bones.
questions.answer: (As printed; "Sate" = State.) X-rays travel in straight lines, penetrate soft tissue but are strongly absorbed by dense, high-Z material such as bone mineral, and expose photographic film / produce shadow images. The differential absorption gives contrast: a crack interrupts the absorbing bone, so the discontinuity shows up on the radiograph.

questions.question: What is the energy of a photon that, when absorbed by a hydrogen atom, could cause an electronic transition from (a) the n =3 state to the n = 5 state and (b) the n = 5 state to the n = 8 state?
questions.answer: (a) E = 13.6(1/3² − 1/5²) = 13.6(1/9 − 1/25) = 13.6 × 0.07111 = 0.97 eV. (b) E = 13.6(1/5² − 1/8²) = 13.6(0.04 − 0.015625) = 0.33 eV. The absorbed photon must match the level spacing exactly.

questions.question: What are the (a) wavelength range and (b) frequency range of the Lyman series and the Balmer series?
questions.answer: (a) Lyman (ends at n = 1): 121.6 nm (from n = 2) down to 91.2 nm (series limit). Balmer (ends at n = 2): 656.3 nm (from n = 3) down to 364.6 nm (limit). (b) f = c/λ: Lyman 2.47×10¹⁵ Hz to 3.29×10¹⁵ Hz; Balmer 4.57×10¹⁴ Hz to 8.23×10¹⁴ Hz.

questions.question: Distinguish between spontaneous and stimulated emission.
questions.answer: Spontaneous emission: an excited atom decays at a random instant (lifetime ≈10⁻⁸ s), releasing a photon of random phase, direction and polarisation, independent of any other photon — ordinary light sources. Stimulated emission: an incident photon of energy hf = E₂ − E₁ triggers the decay, and the emitted photon is identical to the triggering one in phase, frequency, polarisation and direction — coherent amplification, the basis of the laser.

questions.question: Explain why population inversion is necessary in a laser?
questions.answer: In thermal equilibrium N₂ < N₁ (Boltzmann), so absorption exceeds stimulated emission and a passing beam is attenuated. Only with an inversion (N₂ > N₁) does stimulated emission dominate absorption, giving net gain per pass so that the resonator can build up an intense coherent beam.

questions.question: In an optically pumped laser, the light that causes optical pumping is always shorter in wavelength than the laser beam. Explain
questions.answer: Pump photons must lift atoms from the ground state to a level above the upper laser level, so E<sub>pump</sub> > E<sub>laser</sub>; part of that energy is then lost as non-radiative decay into the metastable upper laser level. Since λ = hc/E, the higher energy means the shorter wavelength: λ<sub>pump</sub> < λ<sub>laser</sub>.

questions.question: A hydrogen atom is in its first excited state (n = 2). Calculate (a) the kinetic energy of the electron, (b) the potential energy of the system, and (c) the total energy of the system.
questions.answer: E₂ = −13.6/2² = −3.4 eV. For a Coulomb orbit (virial theorem): (a) K = −E = +3.4 eV; (b) U = 2E = −6.8 eV; (c) E = K + U = −3.4 eV.

questions.question: What are the postulates of Bohr's Model of hydrogen atom? Discuss the importance of this model to explain various series of line spectra in hydrogen atom. Do any of the assumptions of the Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom contradict with the classical Physics? Derive the expression for total energy of electron in nth Bohr orbit and show that- En∝1/n².
questions.answer: Postulates: (i) the electron revolves in certain stationary orbits without radiating; (ii) only orbits with angular momentum mvr = nh/2π are allowed; (iii) radiation is emitted or absorbed only in a jump between orbits, with hf = E<sub>i</sub> − E<sub>f</sub>. Series: combining (iii) with the quantised levels E<sub>n</sub> = −13.6/n² eV gives 1/λ = R<sub>H</sub>(1/p² − 1/n²); p = 1 Lyman (UV), p = 2 Balmer (visible), p = 3 Paschen, p = 4 Brackett, p = 5 Pfund (IR) — each a family of discrete lines, exactly the observed line spectra. Contradiction with classical physics: an accelerated charge must radiate continuously, so the orbiting electron should spiral into the nucleus in ≈10⁻¹¹ s and emit a continuous spectrum; atoms are stable and show lines instead — the stationary-orbit postulate openly contradicts classical electrodynamics. Derivation: ke²/r² = mv²/r ⇒ K = ke²/2r and U = −ke²/r; quantisation mvr = nℏ with v² = ke²/(mr) gives r<sub>n</sub> = n²ℏ²/(mke²) = n²a₀. Then E<sub>n</sub> = K + U = −ke²/2r<sub>n</sub> = −(mk²e⁴/2ℏ²)(1/n²) = −13.6/n² eV ⇒ E<sub>n</sub> ∝ 1/n².

questions.question: How X-rays are produced? State the purpose of cooling fins in the X-ray tube.
questions.answer: Production: thermionic electrons accelerated through tens of kV strike a heavy-metal target (W, Cu). Two mechanisms: (i) bremsstrahlung — deceleration in the nuclear Coulomb field gives a continuous spectrum with cut-off λ<sub>min</sub> = hc/eV; (ii) characteristic lines — inner-shell ionisation followed by outer electrons filling the vacancy gives sharp lines (Kα, Kβ). Cooling fins: only ≈1% of the electron-beam power becomes X-rays, ≈99% becomes heat in the target; the copper anode block with radiating cooling fins (or water cooling) carries this heat away and keeps the target below melting.

questions.question: Explain why X-rays are appropriate in study of crystalline structure material? Write some main properties of X-rays.
questions.answer: Crystal plane spacings are ≈0.1–0.3 nm, the same order as X-ray wavelengths, so a crystal acts as a three-dimensional diffraction grating (Bragg: 2d sinθ = nλ); visible light (400–700 nm) is far too long to diffract from the planes. Measuring the diffraction angles yields the plane spacings and hence the structure. Properties: electromagnetic waves of ≈0.01–10 nm travelling at c in straight lines; uncharged, hence undeflected by electric or magnetic fields; highly penetrating, absorbed more strongly by high-Z material; ionise gases; expose photographic film; cause fluorescence; undergo reflection and diffraction (Bragg); eject photoelectrons and show Compton scattering.

questions.question: What is Laser? Write the characteristics of Laser light. Can a two-level system be used for the production of Laser? Why?
questions.answer: LASER = Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation: a device producing an intense beam of coherent light by stimulated emission in a pumped gain medium placed between resonator mirrors. Characteristics: monochromatic (single λ), coherent (fixed phase relationship), highly directional (divergence ≈ mrad), high intensity and brightness. A two-level system cannot lase: resonant pumping drives absorption and stimulated emission at equal rates, so at best N₂ = N₁ (saturation); the inversion N₂ > N₁ is unreachable and net amplification is impossible. At least three levels (or four) are required.

questions.question: What is pumping? What are the different methods of pumping? Explain optical pumping.
questions.answer: Pumping is the external energy supply that creates the population inversion in the active medium. Methods: optical (flash lamp, laser diode, sunlight), electrical (gas discharge as in He-Ne, injection current in semiconductors), chemical (exothermic reaction products), and thermal/injection schemes. Optical pumping: pump photons of shorter wavelength are absorbed, raising atoms from the ground state to a broad absorption band; fast non-radiative decay then piles them into a metastable upper laser level, building the inversion — e.g. Cr³⁺ in ruby pumped by a xenon flash lamp.

questions.question: What is the principle of Laser? Write the construction and working of Helium-neon laser.
questions.answer: Principle: stimulated emission + population inversion + optical feedback. Construction: a sealed glass tube with He:Ne ≈ 10:1 at ≈1 torr, electrodes for a DC discharge, and two mirrors (one fully reflecting, one ≈99% reflecting) forming the optical resonator. Working: discharge electrons excite He to metastable states (20.61 eV, 19.82 eV) that nearly coincide with Ne levels; collisions transfer the energy selectively and invert the Ne 5s level against 3p (632.8 nm red; also 3.39 μm and 1.15 μm lines). Photons travelling along the axis stimulate further identical emissions on every mirror pass, and the beam exits through the partial mirror.

questions.question: Give some important properties of lasers. Also write the uses of lasers in the field of medicine, defense and communication.
questions.answer: Properties: monochromaticity, coherence, directionality, high intensity, focusability to a diffraction-limited spot, and ultrashort pulsing. Medicine: surgery and laser scalpels (cutting while cauterising), retinal welding, lithotripsy, dermatology. Defense: rangefinders, target designators, missile guidance, LIDAR, laser gyros. Communication: fibre-optic links — coherent, directional light carries enormous bandwidth with low loss — plus free-space and satellite links. Also industry (cutting, welding), barcode scanners, holography and metrology.

questions.question: What is wave number? Derive the expression 1/λ = R<sub>H</sub>(1/p² − 1/n²).
questions.answer: Wave number = 1/λ, the number of waves per unit length (m⁻¹). From Bohr: hf = E<sub>n</sub> − E<sub>p</sub> ⇒ hc/λ = 13.6 eV (1/p² − 1/n²) ⇒ 1/λ = (13.6 × 1.602×10⁻¹⁵)/(6.626×10⁻³⁴ × 2.998×10⁴) × (1/p² − 1/n²) = 1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹ (1/p² − 1/n²) = R<sub>H</sub>(1/p² − 1/n²).

questions.question: Derive the expression for Bohr's radius and develop a general relation for radii of quantized orbits of hydrogen atom.
questions.answer: Force balance ke²/r² = mv²/r together with quantisation mvr = nℏ gives v = nℏ/(mr); substituting, r<sub>n</sub> = n²ℏ²/(mke²) (with k = 1/4πε₀ this is ε₀h²n²/πme²). For n = 1: a₀ = 0.529×10⁻¹⁵ m = 0.529 Å, the Bohr radius. General relation: r<sub>n</sub> = n²a₀, i.e. the radii scale as 1, 4, 9, 16, ...

questions.question: Why are protons and neutrons necessary for the stability of an atomic nucleus?
questions.answer: Protons fix the nuclear charge (the element’s identity) but their mutual Coulomb repulsion would blow a pure-proton nucleus apart. Neutrons contribute the attractive, charge-independent strong nuclear force without adding repulsion, and they space the protons apart; the extra neutrons in heavier nuclei offset the growing Coulomb term. With both species present the Pauli principle also allows more nucleons to bind in paired levels. Stability therefore lies along a valley of definite N/Z ratio.

questions.question: How do isotopes of an element differ and why are these differences significant?
questions.answer: Isotopes have the same Z (same electron shell, same chemistry) but different N, hence different A: they differ in nuclear mass, nuclear spin, stability and radioactivity while behaving identically in chemical reactions. Significance: radioactive isotopes serve as tracers in medicine, biology and industry and as clocks in radiometric dating; mass differences allow physical separation (gaseous diffusion, centrifuges) as for <sup>235</sup>U vs <sup>238</sup>U; different isotopes give heavy water, fusion fuels (D, T) and reactor moderators.

questions.question: Name the two methods of controlling a chain reaction.
questions.answer: (i) Control rods of strong neutron absorbers (cadmium, boron, hafnium) inserted or withdrawn to hold the multiplication factor k at exactly 1; (ii) adjusting the moderator/coolant or adding soluble neutron poisons (e.g. boric acid in the coolant) to change the neutron population, together with reflectors and, in emergencies, scram shutdown.

questions.question: Why is nuclear decay described as spontaneous and random?
questions.answer: Spontaneous: the decay rate is unaffected by temperature, pressure, chemical combination or any external agency — it springs solely from the internal instability of the nucleus. Random: no law determines which particular nucleus decays at which instant; each nucleus only has a fixed probability per unit time λ, so decay is governed by statistics, giving the exponential law for large numbers.

questions.question: Explain what happens during the nuclear fusion process.
questions.answer: Two light nuclei approach close enough (≈10⁻¹⁵ m) for the attractive strong force to overcome their Coulomb repulsion — requiring temperatures ≈10⁷–10⁸ K — and merge into a heavier nucleus. The product’s mass is less than the sum of the ingredients; the defect Δm is released as kinetic energy, E = Δmc². Example: D + T → <sup>4</sup>He + n + 17.6 MeV. Fusion releases more energy per unit mass than fission and powers the stars.

questions.question: How are activity and decay constant related in radioactive materials?
questions.answer: Activity A = |dN/dt| = λN: the decay rate equals the decay constant times the number of undecayed nuclei (unit becquerel, 1 Bq = 1 decay/s). Since N = N₀e⁻λt, the activity falls with the same law, A = A₀e⁻λt, and λ = ln2/T₁/₂.

questions.question: What is meant by binding energy and binding energy per nucleon?
questions.answer: Binding energy is the energy required to dissect a nucleus completely into free protons and neutrons (equivalently, the energy released when it forms): BE = Δmc², with Δm the mass defect. Binding energy per nucleon, BE/A, is the average energy holding each nucleon; it measures nuclear stability and explains why fusion of light and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy (curve peaks ≈8.8 MeV at Fe-56).

questions.question: Why is the concept of half-life important in studying radioactive substances?
questions.answer: The half-life T₁/₂ = ln2/λ characterises a nuclide’s decay rate independently of amount, shape, temperature or history, so one number predicts the remaining fraction N/N₀ = (1/2)^(t/T) at any time. It underlies radiometric dating, medical dose planning and safe storage times, and spans ≈10⁻²² s to 10⁹ years across nuclides, distinguishing fiercely active from nearly stable species.

questions.question: Explain the process of positron emission.
questions.answer: A proton-rich nucleus converts a proton into a neutron: p → n + e⁺ + ν<sub>e</sub>. The positron (anti-electron, +e) and a neutrino are ejected; Z decreases by 1 while A stays the same, e.g. <sup>18</sup><sub>9</sub>F → <sup>18</sup><sub>8</sub>O + e⁺ + ν<sub>e</sub>. The positron soon annihilates with an electron into two 511 keV gamma photons — the signal used in PET imaging.

questions.question: What is radioactivity? State the law of radioactive disintegration. Show that radioactive decay is exponential in nature.
questions.answer: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of α, β or γ radiation from unstable nuclei. Law of disintegration: the rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei, dN/dt = −λN. Integrating, dN/N = −λdt ⇒ ln(N/N₀) = −λt ⇒ N = N₀e⁻λt: the number of undecayed nuclei falls exponentially, halving every T₁/₂ = ln2/λ. Activity A = λN follows the same exponential, and the mean life is 1/λ.

questions.question: Explain the main differences between alpha, beta, and gamma emissions.
questions.answer: Alpha: helium nuclei (<sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He⁺⁺), charge +2e, mass 4 u, speeds ≈0.05c, strongly ionising, least penetrating (stopped by paper), deflected by E and B fields, discrete energies, emitted by heavy nuclei via tunnelling. Beta: fast electrons or positrons, charge ∓e, mass m<sub>e</sub>, speeds up to ≈0.9c, moderate ionisation and penetration (few mm of aluminium), deflected oppositely to alphas, continuous energy spectrum (shared with the neutrino), from weak-interaction nucleon conversion. Gamma: electromagnetic photons, no charge or rest mass, travel at c, weakly ionising but most penetrating (cm of lead or m of concrete), undeflected by fields, discrete energies, emitted when an excited nucleus de-excites.

questions.question: A fission reactor produces energy to drive a generator. Describe briefly how this energy is produced.
questions.answer: Thermal neutrons fission <sup>235</sup>U: n + <sup>235</sup>U → fragments (e.g. Ba + Kr) + 2–3 neutrons + ≈200 MeV, mostly as kinetic energy of the fragments. The fragments stop in the fuel, heating it; the coolant (water, heavy water) carries the heat to a steam generator; steam drives a turbine coupled to an electrical generator. The moderator thermalises fission neutrons, control rods hold k = 1, and the pressure vessel plus shielding contain the radiation — a controlled, self-sustaining chain reaction converting nuclear binding energy into electricity.

questions.question: Define Q-value of a nuclear reaction and its significance.
questions.answer: For a + X → Y + b, the Q-value is Q = (m<sub>a</sub> + m<sub>X</sub> − m<sub>Y</sub> − m<sub>b</sub>)c² = final kinetic energy − initial kinetic energy. Q > 0 (exoergic): mass is converted into kinetic energy and the reaction can yield power (fission, fusion); Q < 0 (endoergic): the projectile must supply a threshold energy. Significance: Q fixes the energy release per reaction, the product speeds, whether a reaction runs spontaneously, and the energy budget of reactors, stars and weapons.

questions.question: Describe the construction and working of GM counter.
questions.answer: Construction: a hollow metal cylinder (cathode) with a thin coaxial tungsten anode wire, filled with argon at ≈0.1 atm plus a quenching vapour (alcohol/bromine), and a thin end window for weakly penetrating radiation; a voltage of ≈900–1200 V is applied. Working: an incoming α, β or γ ionises a gas atom; the electron accelerates to the wire, ionising further atoms in an avalanche (Geiger discharge) that spreads along the whole wire; the resulting pulse is counted electronically. The quenching gas absorbs UV photons and prevents continuous discharge. It counts events with high sensitivity but gives no information on particle energy or type.

questions.question: Discus nuclear reactions induced by neutrons. Why are neutrons preferred to other particles?
questions.answer: (As printed, "Discus" = Discuss.) Neutron-induced reactions: radiative capture (n,γ) producing a heavier isotope; charged-particle emission (n,p), (n,α); elastic and inelastic scattering (n,n); and fission (n,f) in heavy nuclei; plus neutron activation used to make radioisotopes. Neutrons are preferred because they carry no charge: there is no Coulomb barrier to climb, so even thermal neutrons reach the nucleus with high probability, they penetrate deep into matter, and their cross-sections grow as 1/v at low energy — making slow neutrons extremely effective at inducing fission and capture, unlike protons or alphas which must be accelerated to MeV energies.

questions.question: What is a nuclear reaction? Explain nuclear fission and fusion.
questions.answer: A nuclear reaction is any process that changes a nucleus — its composition, energy or both — whether spontaneously (decay) or when a projectile strikes it: a + X → Y + b, conserving charge, nucleon number, energy and momentum. Fission: a heavy nucleus (U, Pu) splits into two medium-mass fragments plus 2–3 neutrons and ≈200 MeV, because the fragments have higher B/A; the released neutrons can sustain a chain reaction (reactors, bombs). Fusion: light nuclei (H, D, T) combine into a heavier nucleus with higher B/A, releasing still more energy per unit mass (stars, H-bomb); it needs ≈10⁷ K to overcome Coulomb repulsion. Both move products toward the peak of the B/A curve near iron.

questions.question: How do the Sun and stars produce energy? What is the proton-proton cycle? Explain with details.
questions.answer: Gravitational contraction heats a stellar core to ≈1.5×10⁷ K at enormous density; there thermonuclear fusion converts hydrogen into helium, and the mass defect powers the star for billions of years. In Sun-like stars the proton-proton cycle dominates: (1) p + p → <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H + e⁺ + ν<sub>e</sub>; (2) <sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>H + p → <sup>3</sup><sub>2</sub>He + γ; (3) <sup>3</sup><sub>2</sub>He + <sup>3</sup><sub>2</sub>He → <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He + 2p. Net: 4p → <sup>4</sup>He + 2e⁺ + 2ν<sub>e</sub> + 26.7 MeV (the positrons annihilate, adding 2×0.511 MeV each). Heavier, hotter stars run the CNO cycle, where C, N, O catalyse the same 4p → He conversion. The released gamma energy diffuses out as starlight.

questions.question: Explain the difference between bosons and fermions and their roles in mediating fundamental forces.
questions.answer: Fermions have half-integer spin (1/2, 3/2, ...) and obey the Pauli exclusion principle, so they build up matter: the quarks and leptons of the Standard Model. Bosons have integer spin (0, 1, 2, ...) and obey Bose–Einstein statistics, so any number can occupy the same state; the gauge bosons (photon, W±, Z, eight gluons) are exchanged between fermions and thereby mediate the electromagnetic, weak and strong forces, while the Higgs boson (spin 0) is the quantum of the mass-giving field. Forces arise because emitting/absorbing a boson transfers energy and momentum between fermions.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the properties of quarks and leptons, the two main categories of fermions in the Standard Model.
questions.answer: Common: both are spin-1/2 point-like fermions with antiparticles, both feel the weak force, and both come in six flavours arranged in three generations. Contrast: quarks carry color charge and therefore feel the strong force, have fractional electric charges (+2/3 e or −1/3 e), and are permanently confined inside hadrons (baryons, mesons); leptons carry no color (no strong interaction), have integer charges (0 or −1 e), and exist as free particles. Quarks combine into protons and neutrons; leptons (electron, muon, tau, three neutrinos) do not.

questions.question: Define the term "lepton" and provide examples of leptons. Explain their fundamental properties and role in the Standard Model of particle physics.
questions.answer: A lepton is a fundamental spin-1/2 fermion that does not feel the strong nuclear force. Examples: the electron e⁻, muon μ⁻, tau τ⁻ and their neutrinos ν<sub>e</sub>, ν<sub>μ</sub>, ν<sub>τ</sub> (plus antiparticles). Properties: point-like with no observed substructure; integer charge (−1 e for charged leptons, 0 for neutrinos); they interact via the weak force (and, if charged, electromagnetism and gravity); lepton number is conserved in each family. Role: leptons form one of the two fermion families of the Standard Model, provide the stable matter of atomic shells (electrons) and mediate beta decay through the weak interaction (e.g. n → p + e⁻ + ν̄<sub>e</sub>).

questions.question: Explain the concept of color charge in quarks and its significance in the strong nuclear force. How does the combination of quarks contribute to the color-neutral nature of protons and neutrons?
questions.answer: Color charge is the charge of the strong interaction: each quark carries one of three colors (red, green, blue) and antiquarks carry anticolors; gluons themselves carry color–anticolor pairs, which makes the strong force self-interacting and confining. Only color-neutral ("white") combinations can exist as free particles: a baryon takes one quark of each color (red + green + blue = white) and a meson pairs a color with its anticolor. The proton (uud) and neutron (udd) each contain three quarks carrying the three different colors, so their net color is zero — they are color-neutral despite being made of colored constituents.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a proton and neutron in terms of its quark composition. How do quarks combine to form a proton and a neutron, and what are the specific types of quarks involved?
questions.answer: Proton = uud: charge 2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1 e; neutron = udd: 2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0. In each, three valence quarks (one of each color) are bound by continual gluon exchange, together with a sea of virtual quark–antiquark pairs and gluons; the binding energy supplies nearly all of the nucleon mass. The specific types are the two lightest quark flavours, up (charge +2/3 e) and down (charge −1/3 e); swapping one u for a d (via the weak force) converts a proton into a neutron and vice versa.

questions.question: Explain the structure of the Standard Model, including the different types of particles and their relationships. How does the model classify fundamental forces?
questions.answer: The Standard Model catalogues all known elementary particles: twelve fermions of matter (six quarks u, d, c, s, t, b and six leptons e, μ, τ, ν<sub>e</sub>, ν<sub>μ</sub>, ν<sub>τ</sub>, arranged in three generations of increasing mass), their antiparticles, and the bosons. Fermions combine into hadrons: baryons (three quarks, e.g. p, n) and mesons (quark–antiquark, e.g. π, K). Forces are classified by their gauge bosons: electromagnetism by the massless photon (quantum electrodynamics, acting on charge), the weak force by the massive W± and Z (flavour change, beta decay), and the strong force by eight massless gluons (quantum chromodynamics, acting on color); the Higgs boson is the quantum of the field that gives particles mass. Electromagnetism and the weak force unify as the electroweak interaction; gravity lies outside the model. Relationships: every force vertex couples a boson to fermion or boson lines, and symmetries SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1) dictate the allowed interactions.

questions.question: Describe in detail all fundamental forces and their associated field particles. What is a boson, and why are bosons referred to as field particles?
questions.answer: Gravitation: weakest, infinite range, acts on all energy; postulated field particle is the graviton (spin 2, not yet observed). Electromagnetic: between charges, infinite range, strength ≈1/137; field particle the massless photon. Weak: responsible for beta decay and flavour change, range ≈10⁻¹⁸ m because its field particles W± and Z are very massive (≈80–91 GeV/c²). Strong: binds quarks in hadrons and nucleons in nuclei, range ≈10⁻¹⁵ m, field particles the eight massless but confined gluons carrying color. A boson is any particle of integer spin obeying Bose–Einstein statistics; gauge bosons are called field particles because each is the quantum of a force field — forces between matter particles arise precisely from the exchange of these field quanta, so the boson carries the interaction from one fermion to another.

questions.question: Describe the operating principle of a Geiger-Müller counter. How does it detect and quantify ionizing radiation, and what are its limitations in terms of measurement range and types of radiation detected?
questions.answer: Principle: a metal cylinder (cathode) with a thin coaxial anode wire is filled with a low-pressure gas (argon plus a quenching vapour) and held at ≈900–1200 V. An incoming α, β or γ photon ionises a gas atom; the freed electron accelerates toward the wire, ionising further atoms in a Townsend avalanche that spreads along the wire as a full Geiger discharge; the quenching gas absorbs UV photons and positive ions so the tube resets. Each event yields an identical voltage pulse, so radiation is quantified by counting pulses per second (count rate ∝ intensity). Limitations: pulse size is independent of the original ionisation, so particle type and energy cannot be determined; a dead time of ≈10⁻⁴ s after each pulse saturates the count at high rates; α and soft β particles need a thin end window; and gamma detection efficiency is low (a few percent) because photons interact weakly with the thin gas.

questions.question: Discuss the uses of a Wilson cloud chamber in particle physics experiments. How does it visualize charged particle tracks, and what factors can affect its performance?
questions.answer: A Wilson cloud chamber holds a vapour (air plus alcohol or water) that is suddenly made supersaturated by an adiabatic expansion of the piston. A charged particle crossing the chamber ionises molecules along its path, and droplets condense on those ions, rendering the track visible and photographable. Uses: discovering the positron, muon and kaons; studying pair production, cosmic-ray showers and nuclear reactions; measuring charge and momentum from the curvature of tracks in an applied magnetic field (curvature direction gives the sign of charge). Performance factors: cleanliness of the gas (dust spoils tracks), timing and depth of the expansion relative to the event, temperature gradient and vapour mixture, uniformity of the magnetic field, illumination and photography, and the sensitive time window (the chamber is only live briefly after each expansion).
